summary: Fernand Ouellet becomes a person entry: the agricultural crisis from 1802 and peasant mentalities as the ground of French-Canadian nationalism and, in large part, the rebellion of 1837–38 (1962–76); his critiques of the Montreal school's Conquest thesis and of the modernist synthesis (1962–85); Creighton's and Labrousse's influence on him; and the critics' answer (quebec_historiography → fernand_ouellet: Paquet and Wallot 1972, Tousignant 1980, Greer 1981). Roster rows for Paquet, Greer, Tousignant, J.-P. Bernard, Normand Séguin and Le Goff on quebec_historiography; the agricultural-crisis and Montreal-school strands are rewritten from read texts; a new strand, 'Interpreting the rebellions of 1837–38'.
authorization: User, 2026-10-14: 'Quebec does need more research as we also probably need Oullet and then some of his critics'. Research: data/extension-2026/quebec-historiography-2026-10-14/evidence-quebec.md.
rationale: Most accounts of Quebec's historiography read for the research (Rudin, Bédard, Gagnon, Fecteau, Dechêne, Ouellet himself) treat the crisis thesis as a pivot of the field's main controversy, though some named accounts do not mention Ouellet (evidence-quebec.md), so Ouellet carries a framework students meet, by the person-entry principle. His own 1962, 1976 and 1985 texts and the critics' 1972, 1980 and 1981 articles were read on Érudit with printed pages; Greer's 1993 book is known only through its reviewers, Le Goff (1974) and Ouellet's 1995 reply to Greer are unread. Maurice Séguin and Lionel Groulx are recommended by the research but await the user's decision; the critique of the Montreal school targets the group entry's strand until then. Dissertation evidence is metadata only.

text_revisions.old: Ouellet and Hamelin’s 1962 agricultural-crisis thesis and Paquet and Wallot’s 1972–73 counter-interpretation, with Wallot’s Quebec ‘qui bougeait’. A dated exchange; titles only.
text_revisions.new: Ouellet and Hamelin’s 1962 thesis that a fall in wheat production from 1802, with population pressure and peasant routine, lay behind French-Canadian nationalism and, ‘en grande partie’, the rebellion of 1837–38; Paquet and Wallot’s 1972 rejection of it as ‘irrecevable’ and their market-rational habitant, with Wallot’s Quebec ‘qui bougeait’; Ouellet’s reply (1976), defending the production-based explanation and disputing his critics’ reading of his argument; Le Goff’s review of the controversy (1974, unread); Tousignant’s critique of Le Bas-Canada (1980); and Greer’s rejection of the ‘atavistic mentality’ explanation (1981). Ouellet (1985) names later entrants (Isbester, McCallum, McInnis, Courville). The 1962, 1972, 1976 and 1980 texts and Greer (1981) were read for the Ouellet person entry. The exchange is not presented as resolving the crisis’s chronology, causes or explanatory reach; Paquet and Wallot themselves doubted the debate was settled.
text_revisions.reason: The strand said 'titles only'; the principal texts were read for the Ouellet entry (evidence-quebec.md §2), and the critics named here are proposed as roster rows. Strand source_ids and person_ids cannot be extended by text_revisions; see strand_list_additions.

text_revisions.old: Séguin, Frégault and Brunet make the Conquest and its economic and national consequences their central problem (titles); Savard groups them by shared ideological outlook.
text_revisions.new: Séguin, Frégault and Brunet make the Conquest and its economic and national consequences their central problem; Savard groups them by shared ideological outlook. Ouellet (1985) calls Séguin the ‘théoricien de l’École néo-nationaliste’, for whom the Conquest decapitated the national bourgeoisie, a thesis Brunet took up in the 1950s; Tousignant (1980) calls Séguin the school’s ‘maître à penser’ and describes the gulf between it and Ouellet.
text_revisions.reason: Adds two in-period francophone readings, read for the Ouellet entry, that name Séguin as the school's theorist; supports the critique edge pe137_ouellet_rel_03 that targets this strand.

strand.title: Interpreting the rebellions of 1837–38
strand.focus: Ouellet’s reading of the rebellion as, in large part, ‘une réponse détournée’ to agricultural crisis and demographic pressure (1962), with a peasantry led by the liberal professions; the national and social readings Ouellet himself describes as polarised (1985: Bernard, Bernier, Bourque, Dubuc, Ouellet, Ryerson); Bernard’s collection on the Patriotes in memory and historiography (1983, unread); and Greer’s rural history of 1837 (1993, unread; through reviews), which reviewers say breaks with Ouellet’s manipulated peasantry.
strand.works: Ouellet and Hamelin (1962); Ouellet, 'Le mythe de « l'habitant sensible au marché »' (1976); Bernard, ed. (1983); Greer (1993)
